segments.summary: An endpoint initially constructs a simple Logger object inside its handler. Moving that construction into get_logger gives operations a reusable supplier, and Depends declares the handler’s need for the supplied Logger. An Annotated[Logger, Depends(get_logger)] alias then makes the declaration shorter to reuse. The provider still returns a new Logger; the improvement is removing repeated construction code from handlers, not keeping one object for the whole application.

segments.label: Deferred email and the process-failure boundary
segments.summary: Sending email can take time, so FastAPI can send the response first and run the background task afterward. Pending tasks are lost if the server crashes. The speaker distinguishes critical work from a password-reset email that the user can request again. Suitability therefore depends on whether the operation can tolerate losing the pending work, not merely on whether deferring it makes the response faster.

segments.label: Send a TestClient request and verify status and JSON
segments.summary: An endpoint test imports TestClient and the application, creates a client, and sends a GET request from a test function. It checks both status 200 and the expected JSON string, "server is running". Running pytest confirms the test passes. Adding an exclamation mark to the endpoint's response makes the same test fail; restoring the response removes the deliberate mismatch.

segments.label: Build an async session factory and yield a session from its context
segments.summary: The setup replaces a synchronous engine with create_async_engine and checks that the database driver supports asynchronous operation. PostgreSQL uses psycopg in this example; other databases may need a different async-compatible driver. An async_sessionmaker bound to the engine provides the session factory, named async_session_local here. An async dependency obtains a session with async with, yields it to the endpoint, and leaves cleanup to the context when its block finishes. FastAPI supplies the yielded session to the route through Depends.

segments.label: Replace a string-returning dependency with a test provider
segments.summary: A simple endpoint uses Depends to obtain a string from a provider. Initially, running the endpoint test prints 'actual user'. A replacement provider returns 'mock user', and the application's dependency_overrides dictionary maps the original provider callable to that replacement callable. Rerunning the test prints 'mock user', demonstrating that FastAPI resolves the declared dependency through the replacement. The example observes the substituted value through printed output; it does not assert that value or restore the override.

segments.label: Extract supplied fields without including omitted defaults
segments.summary: A partial update should contain only fields the client supplied. Calling model_dump(exclude_unset=True) on the request-body model extracts those fields. In the example, the client supplies a new title but omits content. Including every model field would also include content's default None, risking the loss of stored content. Excluding unset fields keeps the supplied title and leaves omitted content out of the extracted update.

segments.label: Trace a Redis cache miss, population, and subsequent hit
segments.summary: The application decides whether to read from Redis or the database. For a profile request, it checks Redis first. When the profile is absent, the application queries the database, stores a copy of the returned profile in Redis, and responds to the caller. A subsequent request checks Redis again and finds the profile, allowing the application to respond without repeating the database query. Reusing cached results can reduce database reads; the actual performance benefit depends on the workload.

segments.label: How expiry and write invalidation trigger fresh reads
segments.summary: A cached project list becomes stale when a new project is added to the database but the cached list remains unchanged. A time to live (TTL) expires the key automatically; the next read then misses and reloads from the database. A 60-second lifetime accepts up to 60 seconds of staleness. Write invalidation instead deletes the affected key when the database changes, so the next read reloads the updated list. Every relevant write path must perform that deletion. Combining expiry with write invalidation limits how long an overlooked stale copy can remain.

segments.label: Replace per-movie review queries with selectinload
segments.summary: Accessing a movie's reviews triggers an additional SELECT when the relationship is lazily loaded. Listing eight movies and accessing reviews for each produces nine queries: one for the movies and eight for their reviews. Adding options(selectinload(Movie.reviews)) to the selection changes the loading strategy. The ORM gathers the selected movie IDs and fetches their reviews together using an IN condition. With engine echo logging enabled, the demonstrated listing goes from nine queries to two: one for movies and one for the associated reviews.

segments.label: Set up a test session and clean it up after yield
segments.summary: A pytest yield fixture combines session setup and cleanup. This example creates tables and test items before yielding the session, then closes the session and drops the tables afterward. Tests receive the session through the fixture and use it directly to create an item. This illustrates fixture cleanup, rather than the outer-transaction isolation pattern taught here.

segments.label: Define an order prediction task using checkout-time inputs
segments.summary: A task record connects the prediction to the examples that support it. Here, each example represents one order, rather than a customer or a day. Two possible targets are checkout-to-doorstep minutes and arrival after the promise fixed at checkout. Predictions are made at checkout, so later dispatch information, the courier’s route and actual delivery cannot serve as inputs. The record also identifies the decision the prediction supports, such as setting a delivery promise or offering an express upgrade, and whether the intended population includes future orders, unseen customers or both.

segments.label: Check how a row and column broadcast into a multiplication table
segments.summary: A two-dimensional row containing 1 through 10 has shape (1, 10), while a column containing the same numbers has shape (10, 1). Their shapes are printed and checked: each aligned dimension either matches or has length 1. Multiplication combines the row and column into a multiplication table with shape (10, 10). Compatible operands can therefore produce a result larger than either input.

segments.label: Selection bias: interpreting only the aircraft that returned
segments.summary: Selection bias arises when observed information does not represent the population intended for study. In the aircraft example, officers examined returning planes, which had many bullet holes in their bodies and wings but fewer near their engines. They proposed protecting the areas with the most observed hits. Abraham Wald instead argued for protecting the areas with few observed hits: aircraft hit in the engine were not returning to be counted. The observed damage described surviving aircraft, not all aircraft exposed to fire. Missing observations therefore changed the interpretation of the collected evidence.

segments.label: Use known past values to construct prediction-time features
segments.summary: To predict sales at time t+1 while currently at t, construct features from known values at t, t−1, and earlier. For a prediction of sales at t, the corresponding features start at t−1 and continue backward. Moving this boundary for each prediction produces feature vectors paired with their targets. The governing constraint is availability: using information not yet known would leak future information into an earlier prediction.

segments.label: How aggregate improvement hides language-slice performance gaps
segments.summary: In a synthetic fraud fixture, underlying fraud is equal across languages, but an English-centric description-quality score is lower for Hindi and Hinglish. Adding this score improves overall detection. Regional flag rates remain nearly equal because languages are evenly distributed across regions. Language slices reveal a different pattern: the model detects 33.5% of fraud overall, about one-fifth of English-language fraud, over 40% of Hindi-language fraud, and more than half of Hinglish-language fraud. The example illustrates how aggregate improvement and balanced regional rates can coexist with uneven performance across other important slices.

segments.label: Recognize overfitting from training and validation loss
segments.summary: Overfitting occurs when a model fits training observations closely but generalizes poorly. A one-input, one-output example illustrates a fit that follows the training values too closely. Comparing training and validation loss provides evidence: as training continues, training loss can fall while validation loss rises. Since lower loss means better performance for both, this divergence indicates worsening generalization despite improving training performance.

segments.label: Trace tensor operations to a scalar output and inspect its gradients
segments.summary: PyTorch records operations involving a tensor with requires_grad=True in a computation graph. The example adds 2 to a three-value tensor, squares the result, multiplies by 2, and takes the mean to produce a scalar. Calling backward() on that scalar computes derivatives with respect to the original tensor, available in its .grad attribute. Intermediate tensors carry gradient-function information corresponding to their operations. Without gradient tracking, the demonstrated backward call fails. The explanation connects differentiation through the graph to the chain rule and notes that a scalar output needs no explicit argument to backward().

segments.label: Compare cross-entropy losses using raw class logits and class-index targets
segments.summary: The example constructs CrossEntropyLoss and supplies raw class logits rather than separately applying softmax. For the chosen class-index contract, the target identifies the correct class directly. The output tensor has one row for one example and three columns for three classes. Two sets of logits are evaluated against target class zero: the set assigning the highest score to the correct class produces the lower scalar loss. The example demonstrates why output and target representations must be chosen before interpreting the loss value.

segments.label: Training and validation use two separate controls
segments.summary: PyTorch's train and eval methods change the behavior of mode-sensitive layers such as dropout and batch normalization. Validation uses eval to select evaluation behavior and no_grad to prevent gradient-graph recording; these controls serve different purposes. Each training epoch starts in training mode and performs the forward pass, loss calculation, gradient clearing, backward pass, and optimizer step. The separate validation block switches to evaluation mode, disables graph recording, and computes validation loss without updating weights. Starting the next epoch in training mode restores training behavior.

segments.label: Guard a Python script’s entry point so imports do not invoke it
segments.summary: Python assigns __name__ the value "__main__" when a file runs directly and the module’s name when it is imported. Using two Python files, the demonstration first shows that unguarded top-level statements execute during import. It then moves the executable work into a main function and calls that function behind if __name__ == "__main__":. Direct execution still invokes main, but importing the file no longer invokes that guarded function. The guard controls the entry-point call; it does not prevent other top-level statements from executing during import.

segments.label: Create a supplied workflow, trigger it, and inspect step logs
segments.summary: A Java/Gradle workflow template creates a YAML file under .github/workflows. Its event configuration triggers execution for pushes to the configured branch and pull requests targeting that branch. The job groups steps that check out the repository, prepare Java, and execute supplied commands. Reusable actions are referenced with uses; commands are executed with run. Creating a matching pull request triggers the workflow. Opening the completed run reveals job setup, checkout, Java setup, build output reporting success, and automatic cleanup. Inspecting these step logs connects the declared workflow to what actually executed.

segments.label: Assign account permission sets to a group and sign in
segments.summary: The demonstration assigns a management group to an AWS account with administrator and view-only permission sets. A user in that group receives access through those assignments. The user accepts an invitation, sets a password, and registers an authenticator app for MFA. In the access portal, the user selects the account, sees the assigned permission sets, and opens the management console with ViewOnlyAccess. The console identifies the selected access, but no intended operation is tested.

segments.label: How the AWS CLI collects a full listing across service pages
segments.summary: A paginated EC2 listing can require multiple API requests. The AWS CLI retrieves the first page, checks the service response for more results, and requests subsequent pages until the service indicates that none remain. It assembles the results in memory and returns the complete list, so the operator does not have to retrieve each service page manually.

segments.label: Attach an existing IAM role and confirm an allowed request
segments.summary: The demonstration uses DemoRoleForEC2, an existing role with IAM read-only access. In the EC2 console, the presenter opens Actions > Security > Modify IAM role, selects the role, saves the change, and confirms the assignment in Security. Running aws iam list-users then returns user information without running aws configure. This establishes a successful request after attachment, but does not check caller identity or test a denied operation.

segments.label: Configure workflow authentication and inspect a successful AWS access test
segments.summary: The workflow requests permission to generate a GitHub OIDC token, then uses the AWS credentials action to assume a preconfigured IAM role and configure temporary AWS credentials. A bucket-listing step tests access to the target AWS account. After pushing the workflow, the demonstration opens its GitHub Actions run and inspects the successful bucket-listing result. This demonstrates authentication without stored, long-lived AWS access keys; it does not establish that unapproved workflows are rejected.

segments.label: How target tracking adds capacity toward a CPU utilization target
segments.summary: Target tracking adjusts capacity toward a chosen metric target, much like a thermostat maintains a temperature setting. In this example, average CPU utilization has a 50% target. Increased traffic raises utilization to 75%, and target tracking determines that adding five instances would bring utilization back toward the target. Five additional instances is the outcome of this example, not a fixed response for every workload.

segments.label: Preview and apply count-based ECR lifecycle rules
segments.summary: ECR lifecycle policies help remove older build images using defined retention criteria. This example uses development, staging and production tags, including moving tags, to distinguish image groups. The creator opens the lifecycle-rule preview interface, assigns rule priorities and selects tagged images by prefix and image count. A separate rule selects untagged images using a count threshold. The example then applies the lifecycle policy. These counts illustrate the mechanism; use the supplied approved criteria for your repository. The demonstrated selection does not establish whether an eligible image digest is still needed for deployment or rollback.

segments.label: Locate explicit-deny and missing-allow evidence with the IAM Policy Simulator
segments.summary: The IAM Policy Simulator tests selected operations against policies associated with an existing identity. In the example, user Daniel has an allow for all S3 actions and a separate explicit deny for CreateBucket. Simulating CreateBucket returns a denial, and Show Statement identifies the denying statement: an applicable explicit deny takes precedence over an allow. GetObject and DeleteObject return allowed results, with their supporting allow statement available for inspection. Simulated DynamoDB operations return implicit denials because the identity has no permissions granting those actions. These results distinguish an explicit deny from a missing allow; they do not establish that every constraint affecting an actual request has been evaluated.

segments.label: Execute a shell-script document on two selected EC2 instances
segments.summary: The demonstration selects AWS-RunShellScript in Run Command, supplies commands to create a file and a Linux user, and manually selects two EC2 instances. It disables S3 output storage, submits the document, and reports successful overall and detailed status. The presenter then connects to one instance and checks for the created file and user. This illustrates document execution and a check of effects on one node, not a complete record of every target’s invocation status and output. Disabling S3 output storage is a demonstration choice, not a requirement for executing the document.

segments.label: Detect noncanonical formatting with terraform fmt -check; repair it with terraform fmt
segments.summary: Terraform provides a canonical formatting style. The demonstration changes indentation while leaving the declaration syntactically correct, then uses terraform fmt -check to identify the file needing correction. Running terraform fmt repairs the formatting. A formatting check can support continuous integration by enforcing a consistent style, but it is distinct from configuration validation.

segments.label: Configure an SNS email notification route and understand subscription confirmation
segments.summary: The instructor configures an SNS topic and email endpoint for an alarm notification action, reviews the configuration, and creates the alarm. He explains that the recipient must confirm the email subscription before notifications can arrive, but does not demonstrate confirmation or receipt. He also suggests lowering the threshold to test delivery; for this exercise, keep evaluation unchanged and use the supplied test alarm notification.

segments.label: Why a network ACL can permit a request but block its response
segments.summary: Security groups are stateful: an allowed incoming request can receive return traffic. Network ACLs are stateless and evaluate inbound and outbound traffic separately. They can deny specified IP addresses or CIDR ranges. In the example, inbound traffic is allowed, but an outbound destination-deny rule prevents the response from leaving. Receiving a request therefore does not establish that the response path is permitted.

segments.label: How baselines and managed-node targets guide patch scans and installs
segments.summary: Patch Manager uses patch baselines to determine which available patches are applicable and approved. Operations can run on demand or on a schedule and target Systems Manager managed nodes, including through key-value targeting. A scan checks applicable patches against the baseline and reports noncompliance when required patches are missing. An install applies approved patches with the aim of bringing the node into compliance with the defined baseline. For this task, use the already-approved configuration rather than creating new baselines or schedules. Predefined baselines are examples, not recommended best practices.

segments.label: Set prevent_destroy and observe a destruction error
segments.summary: Setting prevent_destroy = true in a resource's lifecycle block causes Terraform to reject a change that would destroy that resource. The demonstrated change produces an “instance cannot be destroyed” error. The presenter explains that permitting the destruction would require removing the lifecycle rule. This protection depends on the rule remaining in the configuration; it is not permanent protection after removal.

segments.label: Why a completed deployment still needs a live smoke check
segments.summary: A deployment operation can finish successfully while the application fails at startup or cannot connect to its database. A smoke check tests basic live behavior immediately after deployment. For a web application, checks might include an expected HTTP 200 response from the homepage, a successful login using test credentials, or a response from a health endpoint. These checks are deliberately simple and fast; the presenter recommends that they finish within one or two minutes. They verify basic functionality rather than providing comprehensive testing.

segments.label: Enable S3 lock-file locking and test a competing apply
segments.summary: The presenter enables S3 lock-file locking with use_lockfile = true and reinitializes the backend. During an apply awaiting approval, the S3 bucket contains a .tflock object. After the operation completes, the state object remains and the lock object disappears. Following a destruction step, the presenter starts another apply and leaves approval pending. A competing apply in a second terminal fails with an error acquiring the state lock. Once the first apply completes, the competing operation can run again and reports that the infrastructure matches the configuration. This demonstrates coordination between Terraform writers without disabling locking.

segments.label: Structure a factual incident record and accountable follow-up
segments.summary: Post-incident analysis records impact, response actions, contributing causes and follow-up work. A blameless account focuses on systems and processes rather than faulting individuals. A useful structure includes an executive summary, incident details, a timeline, lessons learned and action items. Claims about severity need verifiable evidence. Follow-up actions need clear owners, priorities, tracking and a verifiable completion state; they should include prevention rather than only mitigation. Completion status or target dates, followed by later review, help keep those actions accountable.

segments.label: Inspect integer and float values with type()
segments.summary: An integer is a whole number, while a decimal literal such as 3.14 produces a float. Assigning 3 to num and displaying type(num) identifies its type as int. Reassigning num to 3.14 and displaying its type again identifies float. type(value) reports the type of the value currently assigned, rather than a permanent type attached to the variable name.

segments.label: Recognize int, float, str, and bool values
segments.summary: Python’s int type represents whole numbers, including negative integers and zero. The str type represents text enclosed in single or double quotation marks; quoted digits are text too. Either quotation style can surround text containing the other kind of quotation mark. The bool values are True and False, with capital initials. These reserved words cannot be variable names. Decimal literals such as 1.23 produce float values.

segments.label: Return calculated areas, store them, and combine them
segments.summary: An area function initially displays length multiplied by width. Although the apartment and yard areas appear on screen, those displayed numbers are not supplied as calculated results for the caller to combine. Changing the function to return length * width lets the caller store the results in house and yard, then add them to obtain 3,500 square feet. Return also stops the current function call: a display instruction placed after it is never reached. Moving that instruction before return allows the function to display the area and still supply its calculated value to the caller.

segments.label: Recognise block membership and repair inconsistent indentation
segments.summary: Indentation determines which statements belong to an if body. Statements aligned within that body share its condition; an unindented statement following it is outside the body. The example uses x = 10 and compares x with 5. Giving statements in the same body different indentation produces errors; aligning them consistently repairs the structure. Although consistent two-space indentation can work, use four spaces per level.

segments.label: Build indented bodies and add a deeper nested block
segments.summary: An if header ends with a colon, and its indented statements run only when its condition is true. Moving a following statement into or out of that indentation changes whether it belongs to the conditional body. Inconsistent spacing produces an indentation error. Tabs and spaces are different characters, and mixing them can fail even when their alignment looks similar. Use four spaces per level rather than the alternative widths discussed. An if inside another if introduces a deeper body, indented another four spaces.

segments.label: Import math and calculate a square root
segments.summary: An initial attempt to use sqrt without the module name fails. Importing math and calling math.sqrt(25) produces a value that is stored and printed as 5.0. A second calculation uses 15 to demonstrate the same operation with another positive input. Although the presenter initially calls sqrt an inbuilt function, the demonstrated interface is the standard-library function math.sqrt.

segments.label: Access values in a list of lists using successive indices
segments.summary: A list can hold other lists as its elements. Separate lists of drinks, dinner items, and desserts are placed inside a list named food. The inner lists need not contain the same number of items. Selecting food[0] retrieves the drinks list; adding another index, food[0][0], retrieves coffee. Changing the outer index selects a different inner list: food[1][2] selects hot dog from the dinner list. Each pair of brackets selects one level deeper.

segments.label: Save a Python script and invoke it from a terminal
segments.summary: Create hello.py, enter print("hello world"), and save the file before running it. The editor’s unsaved-change indicator helps confirm that edits have been saved. Running the file with the editor’s play button displays hello world in its built-in terminal. The same saved script can be run directly by entering python hello.py in that terminal: the executable name comes first, followed by the script path.

segments.label: Remove surrounding whitespace with text.strip()
segments.summary: Calling text.strip() removes leading and trailing whitespace from entered text. The example accepts hello surrounded by spaces and displays hello after applying strip(). Without that call, the surrounding spaces remain. This cleanup is useful before comparing an entered label with an expected value.

segments.label: Encode a Python string as UTF-8 bytes
segments.summary: The encode method converts a string into bytes using an encoding. Calling encode() without an argument uses UTF-8 by default. The example encodes "hello python" and identifies the resulting bytes value by the b prefix in its displayed representation.

segments.label: Traverse corresponding list values with zip
segments.summary: Two lists are compared at corresponding positions, first using indexes and then using zip. Zip pairs their elements into tuples: (1, 1), (2, 1), (3, 3), and (4, 7). The longer list’s trailing 9 is omitted because it has no partner. Reversing the inputs reverses the order of values within each tuple. Adding a third list with only two elements limits the result to two tuples, each containing three values. Finally, a for loop assigns each pair to two variables and uses an indented conditional body to display whether the values match.

segments.label: Import Counter and inspect element counts
segments.summary: Import Counter from collections to use it directly. Passing a string counts its characters; passing a list counts repeated values. The examples also supply existing counts through a dictionary and keyword arguments. Displayed results associate each element with its count. Counter has its own type, but its element-to-count structure is a mapping.

segments.label: Compare ordinary string display with repr()
segments.summary: Comparing str() and repr() shows why a representation can reveal details that ordinary display hides. Both produce the same displayed result for the example list. For the sample string, repr() includes surrounding quotation marks, while str() does not.

segments.label: Read an enclosing binding and update it with nonlocal
segments.summary: An outer function binds a variable to 10 and calls an inner function that reads that enclosing value. Adding an ordinary assignment inside the inner function creates a local binding instead: the inner function reports 20, while the outer function still reports 10. Declaring the name nonlocal before assigning redirects the update to the existing enclosing binding, so both functions report 20.

segments.label: Read the exception, locate the failing frame, then trace its callers
segments.summary: Begin with the final line of the traceback: it names the exception type and gives an explanatory message, which may need careful interpretation. The frame immediately above it identifies the location of the failure through a file name, line number, function name and source statement. In this example, that location is line four of count.py, inside count_to. The preceding frames record the surrounding function calls. The deepest frame identifies where the exception occurred; frames farther outward provide calling context. The immediate failing operation is not necessarily the place that needs changing, so inspect the callers too.

segments.label: Place breakpoint() before a suspected problem
segments.summary: A breakpoint marks a place where execution pauses so you can investigate the program. The presenter places one inside a function and explains the older approach of importing pdb and calling pdb.set_trace(). Python 3.7 introduced breakpoint() as a shorter built-in call that invokes the same pdb behavior by default.

segments.label: Replace a shared default list with a None guard
segments.summary: An employee-list helper appends a name and displays the list. Passing an existing list updates that list as intended. However, two calls that omit the list accumulate both names in the same default list, rather than starting separately. Default values are evaluated once when the function is defined, so later calls reuse the mutable object. The repair changes the default to None and creates an empty list inside an if employee_list is None branch. The repaired function is written but not executed in this range.

segments.label: Order numbers using an absolute-value key
segments.summary: Ordinary numeric sorting places negative values before positive values. Passing abs as the key function changes the comparison to each number's absolute value: its distance from zero. The sorted result therefore orders the original numbers by magnitude, retaining their signs rather than replacing them with their comparison keys.

segments.label: Place FileNotFoundError before a broader handler
segments.summary: Opening a file with an incorrect filename produces FileNotFoundError. A broad handler replaces the traceback with a missing-file message, but also gives that misleading message for an undefined name. Restricting the handler to FileNotFoundError leaves the NameError unmatched. Adding an Exception handler below it provides a separate, broader response. Putting that broader handler first would prevent the missing-file branch from running. Finally, binding the caught exception with as e allows its error message to be displayed.

segments.label: Expand a list or dictionary into function-call arguments
segments.summary: A function accepts x and y and prints each value. Rather than pass two list elements through separate indexing expressions, a call uses * to expand the list [21, 75] into positional arguments. The function receives x as 21 and y as 75. A second call uses ** to expand a dictionary containing x: 5 and y: 6 into keyword arguments, producing the corresponding values.

segments.label: Collect variable positional arguments into a tuple with *args
segments.summary: An addition function with two parameters rejects a third positional argument. Replacing those parameters with *args lets the function collect its positional arguments into a tuple. The function then iterates over that tuple, accumulates a total, and returns the sum, allowing calls with different numbers of arguments. The collecting parameter can have another name, such as nums; args is the conventional choice.

segments.label: Define an empty class and create two distinct instances
segments.summary: An empty class still needs an indented body; pass supplies that body without adding behavior. The Employee class acts as a blueprint, while two calls create two separate Employee instances. Printing the instances produces object representations with different memory locations, illustrating that they are distinct objects.

segments.label: See how write mode creates a file or truncates an existing one
segments.summary: A file opened for reading cannot be written to. Opening test2.txt with "w" creates it even when no text is written; if the file already exists, that mode discards its existing contents. The demonstration then writes text and shows that successive write calls on the same open file place their text back to back. Append mode is briefly identified as an alternative that avoids replacing existing contents.

segments.label: Extend inherited initialization with super().__init__()
segments.summary: A Developer needs the first name, last name and pay accepted by Employee, plus a programming language. Its own __init__ delegates the shared arguments through super().__init__ rather than duplicating Employee's initialization logic, then stores the programming language. Creating a Developer and displaying its email and programming language confirms that both inherited and derived initialization ran. In this single-base example, the delegated initialization is Employee's implementation.

segments.label: Distinguish shared class attributes from instance attributes
segments.summary: Class variables store attributes shared among instances, whereas instance variables can hold individual values such as an employee’s name, email, and pay. A common annual raise amount is a candidate for a class variable because the same amount applies to all employees, even if it changes from year to year.

segments.label: Load a JSON string into Python values with json.loads
segments.summary: A JSON string contains an object whose students entry holds an array of objects. JSON strings use double quotation marks. After importing the standard-library json module, json.loads converts the string into a Python dictionary. Dictionary key access retrieves the students collection, and indexing retrieves its first item. The result is Python data that can be accessed using familiar collection operations.

segments.label: Define __repr__ and __str__ for distinct display purposes
segments.summary: Special methods customize built-in object behavior. Their names have double underscores on both sides, often called “dunder.” An Employee instance initially has an unhelpful default display. Defining __repr__ gives it an unambiguous, developer-oriented string containing its first name, last name, and pay in a construction-like form. When __str__ is absent, str and ordinary printing fall back to __repr__. Adding __str__ supplies a more convenient user-facing string containing the employee’s full name and email address. Both methods return strings rather than displaying messages themselves. Calling repr or str selects the corresponding representation; the demonstration also compares these calls with calling the special methods directly.

segments.label: Replace explicit file closure with with
segments.summary: Context managers manage resource setup and cleanup. An explicit open, write, and close sequence requires remembering to close the file. Using with for the file operation removes that separate cleanup step: the file closes when the work finishes, including when an error occurs during that work.

segments.label: Copy an image using binary reads and writes
segments.summary: Nested with statements open a source for reading and a destination for writing. After copying a text file, the example attempts to copy a JPEG in text mode and encounters a decoding error. Changing the modes to rb and wb makes the operations read and write bytes instead of text. The example then copies the image in chunks: each read supplies bytes to write, and the loop reads another chunk until none remain. The copied image is opened to check the result.

segments.label: Create a local module and call its helpers
segments.summary: A new Python file named example holds a pi value and functions for squaring, cubing, circumference and circle area. The main script imports example, accesses example.pi and calls functions through the module name. Squaring 3 produces 9, and cubing it produces 27. Keeping these definitions in a separate file separates reusable calculations from the calling script.

segments.label: Import a sibling helper with either import form
segments.summary: The file my_module.py contains statements, a variable and a find_index helper that returns a matching position or -1 when no match exists. A sibling script imports my_module and calls my_module.find_index with a course list and the target 'Math', returning 1. The initial import also executes the module's diagnostic print statement. An alias shortens the module-qualified call; from my_module import find_index instead binds the helper directly, allowing find_index to be called without the module prefix.

segments.label: Compare direct execution and importing with the __main__ guard
segments.summary: Running first_module directly gives its __name__ the value "__main__". When second_module imports it, first_module's __name__ is "first_module", while the directly executed second_module has __name__ equal to "__main__". Initially, an unguarded print in first_module executes during import. Moving that action into a main function and calling it under if __name__ == "__main__": preserves the output during direct execution but prevents that call during import. The guard controls the actions inside its body; it does not stop the module from being imported.

segments.label: Inspect Python's module search locations with sys.path
segments.summary: Python uses a list of search locations to find modules by name. Importing sys and displaying sys.path reveals the directories searched by the interpreter. The demonstration prints this list and explains that Python searches its locations in order.

segments.label: Using random.random() and understanding its bounds
segments.summary: The random module is suitable for dummy data and games, but not for security-sensitive randomness; secrets is recommended for that purpose. After importing random, assigning random.random() to a variable produces a floating-point value that can equal 0.0 but cannot equal 1.0. Repeated runs demonstrate generating values within those bounds.

segments.label: Chain two strings without concatenating lists
segments.summary: Chaining two string inputs produces the characters from the first string, followed by those from the second. The combined traversal is an iterator: items can be retrieved and processed one at a time rather than first constructing a concatenated list. This avoids storing an additional list of all the combined items.

segments.label: Distinguish a failed assertion from an unexpected exception
segments.summary: An unsuccessful equality assertion records a failure; raising an unexpected ValueError records an error. Both outcomes are unsuccessful, but they describe different problems: an unmet checked expectation versus an unexpected exception during execution. An assertion that correctly expects an exception can pass. Start diagnosis with the specific test case, exception type and result category, then use the traceback and test intent to understand the appropriate repair.

segments.label: Repair a generated discount helper using expected results
segments.summary: A generated discount helper runs successfully and returns 80 for a price of 100 with a 20% discount. That result hides a mistake: the helper subtracts 20 as a fixed amount rather than calculating 20% of the price. With a price of 200, it returns 180 instead of the required 160. The repair calculates the discount amount as price multiplied by discount divided by 100, then subtracts that amount. Assertions for both expected results pass after the repair. Generated code and one passing test are not enough to establish correctness; acceptance needs evidence that the behavior matches the requirements.

segments.label: Sketch a wireframe using placeholders and section labels
segments.summary: The presenter sketches a website home page using basic representations rather than finished content. A circle marked L stands for the logo, and boxes represent menu entries, with shading indicating the current selection. A large banner area includes arrows and dots to represent controls for moving between images. Below it, a crossed box marks an image location, a title area indicates a heading, and lines stand for description text. Labels identify the menu, banner, and about-us section so someone else can understand the sketch. These website elements are example choices, not requirements for every screen.

segments.label: How moderator prompts elicit attitudes and opinions
segments.summary: A focus group brings together participants recruited against research objectives. The explanation describes groups of six to ten people, sometimes recruited through agencies offering rewards. A moderator prompts participants to share product opinions or emotional reactions to advertising. Indirect prompts, such as imagining brands as animals, can help participants express feelings that direct questions might not uncover.

segments.label: Redirecting a dominant speaker and inviting quieter participants
segments.summary: During a discussion of airline inconveniences, one participant gives an extended baggage account that drifts into train travel. The moderator acknowledges the contribution and redirects the discussion to another participant. A second example shows the moderator inviting a quieter participant to contribute and asking her to elaborate. The explanation also encourages exchanges between participants when they begin engaging with one another. These interventions create space for more voices rather than allowing one account to occupy the discussion.

segments.label: Assess likelihood and impact to place risks on a risk matrix
segments.summary: A hypothetical road-crossing example separates likelihood from impact, called consequence in the explanation. Infrequent bicycles represent low likelihood and low impact; more frequent bicycles increase likelihood without changing impact. Infrequent trucks represent low likelihood but high impact, while frequent trucks represent high likelihood and high impact. A risk matrix places likelihood on one axis and impact on the other, then assigns a risk level at their intersection. In this example, the low–low combination is low risk, the two mixed combinations are medium risk, and the high–high combination is high risk. These levels belong to the illustrated matrix rather than a universal scoring rule.

segments.label: Distinguish power from interest and interpret the four quadrants
segments.summary: The Influence-Interest Matrix separates a stakeholder’s power to affect an outcome from their interest in that outcome. Power can come from providing resources, making decisions, or influencing others; interest means how much the stakeholder cares about the result. A stakeholder can be high on one dimension and low on the other. In the construction example, a sponsor may occupy the high-power, high-interest corner, while community members who are not directly affected may occupy the low-power, low-interest quadrant. Each combination suggests a different approach: manage high-power, high-interest stakeholders closely; keep high-power, low-interest stakeholders satisfied; keep low-power, high-interest stakeholders informed; and monitor low-power, low-interest stakeholders with less intensive engagement.

segments.label: Manage speaking turns with input signals and a silent start
segments.summary: A facilitator can help keep a complex discussion on time and on track by letting participants signal the kind of contribution they want to make. In this example, yellow cards indicate questions, green cards indicate answers or clarification, blue cards indicate comments or opinions, and red cards indicate observations about the discussion. These signals help the facilitator choose whom to invite next rather than relying only on raised hands. The presenter prioritizes clarification questions; this is an example approach, not a rule for every meeting. A second technique, a silent start, gives participants two or three minutes to think individually and write notes before discussion begins, so they arrive with contributions prepared.

segments.label: Discuss competing stakeholder concerns before revising a proposal
segments.summary: A facilitator proposes another workshop in two weeks and invites participants to express support or disagreement. Participants raise different concerns: timing, accommodating people already present, pressure from a strongly expressed preference, preserving conflict-resolution content, and availability across time zones. The facilitator gathers and summarizes these concerns, then proposes a scheduling poll and an agenda participants can add to, with conflict resolution included. A further response check suggests support for the revised proposal, but does not establish that every concern has been resolved. The exchange illustrates how discussion of participants’ goals and constraints can inform a revised proposal rather than treating initial support as sufficient.

segments.label: Build a job-application BPMN model with an interview decision
segments.summary: A hypothetical job-application process is represented in a BPMN editor. A start event connects through tasks for creating and submitting an application, attending an interview, reviewing an offer, and submitting acceptance forms, ending with the offer accepted. Sequence flows connect the activities. A gateway named “Called for interview” is then inserted after application submission. Its yes route continues to the interview, while its no route leads to an application-rejected end event. Labeling the outgoing flows makes the routing explicit.

segments.label: Build a decision tree with choices, outcome branches, and endpoints
segments.summary: A decision tree maps related choices and their possible outcomes through branches. Begin with the main decision and draw a branch for each possible action, then extend those branches to further possibilities. The example starts with choosing work or fishing. Work leads to keeping or losing a job; fishing leads to catching or not catching fish. The example assigns illustrative probabilities to these outcomes. Squares represent decisions, circles represent uncertain outcomes, and triangles mark endpoints where no further choices or uncertain outcomes remain.

segments.label: Determine minimum and maximum counts at each relationship end
segments.summary: Cardinality describes how many instances of one entity can relate to an instance of another. A circle represents zero, a bar represents one, and a crow’s-foot represents many. Determine the minimum and maximum separately in each direction. In the customer–order example, each order relates to exactly one customer, while a customer may have zero or many orders. In the order–order item example, each item relates to exactly one order, while each order has one or many items. These counts express the business rules assumed in the examples.

segments.label: Recognize one-to-many and many-to-many from matching values
segments.summary: Comparing matching CustomerID values illustrates relationship types. Two customer tables with unique CustomerID values on both sides illustrate one-to-one. Customers with unique CustomerID values matched to orders with repeated CustomerID values illustrate one-to-many; an individual customer having only one order does not change that classification. Reversing the sides gives many-to-one. In the final example, CustomerID repeats in both customer-segment records and orders, illustrating many-to-many: multiple orders can match multiple segment records for the same customer. These examples illustrate matching patterns; permitted counts must still follow the business rules.

segments.label: Join employee tables using matching employee IDs
segments.summary: A query combines EmployeeDemographics and EmployeeSalary using an ON condition that equates their EmployeeID columns. Writing JOIN alone means INNER JOIN. The resulting output includes columns from both tables for matching employee IDs. The explanation describes these matches as the tables' common or overlapping data; the match is determined by EmployeeID, not by equality of every column.

segments.label: Keep only matching customer and order rows
segments.summary: An INNER JOIN returns matching rows and excludes rows without a match. In the example, Customers is called the left table and Orders the right table, based on their positions in the query. Regardless of those positions, the result contains only matches between the two tables.

segments.label: Find missing and present values with IS NULL and IS NOT NULL
segments.summary: A customer-score example demonstrates two missing-value checks. Starting with five customers, WHERE score IS NULL returns the customer whose score is missing. The missing-value test uses IS NULL, not equality. Changing the condition to WHERE score IS NOT NULL returns customers with recorded scores. These conditions filter the returned rows; they do not change the stored scores.

segments.label: LEFT OUTER JOIN: retain customers without orders
segments.summary: A left outer join keeps matching combinations and preserves unmatched rows from the left table. The table to preserve belongs in FROM; the right table follows LEFT JOIN. To retrieve all customers with any matching orders, the demonstration keeps customers on the left and changes the join to LEFT JOIN. The resulting customer list includes Martin and Peter, whose order fields contain NULL because no orders match. LEFT JOIN is the shorter spelling of LEFT OUTER JOIN. Left-table preservation reflects the query's requirement, not a table's inherent business importance.

segments.label: Trace a RIGHT JOIN: preserve orders and identify NULL customer fields
segments.summary: With Customers on the left and Orders on the right, the right join keeps every order and attaches matching customer information. Orders for customer IDs 1, 2, and 3 have matching customers. An order referencing customer ID 6 has no matching customer, so its left-side customer fields are NULL. The order remains in the result despite that missing match.

segments.label: FULL OUTER JOIN: matching rows and missing-side NULLs
segments.summary: A FULL OUTER JOIN retains matching combinations and unmatched rows from both tables. In the customers-and-orders example, an existing query is changed to FULL JOIN, an equivalent name for FULL OUTER JOIN. Matching customer and order data appear together. Customers without orders remain in the result with NULL in the order columns. An order without a matching customer also remains, with NULL in the customer columns. Neither table is the sole side whose unmatched rows are preserved.

segments.label: Connect the Customers text file and check its separator
segments.summary: In Tableau’s Connect pane, select Text File, choose the Customers file, and open it to reach the Data Source page. Text File Properties provides the file’s separator setting. The example uses a semicolon; if the source file changes to a comma separator, Tableau’s setting must change to match.

segments.label: Compare options using shared criteria, weighted scores, and justified trade-offs
segments.summary: A car-selection example introduces a comparison table with shared criteria and a common 1–5 performance scale. Higher scores mean better performance against the criterion: a high cost score means inexpensive, not a higher purchase price. The example first adds unweighted scores, then introduces importance weights because criteria need not matter equally. Each option’s criterion score is multiplied by that criterion’s weight, and the weighted scores are summed. The resulting totals are 75, 55, and 35, supporting the highest-scoring option under that assessment. A facilities-management supplier example then explains a trade-off: although cost has the greatest importance, an option with a poorer cost score can lead overall because of stronger service and easier termination. A supported recommendation considers all agreed criteria and their weights rather than choosing solely on price.

segments.label: An admissions website recommendation with supporting financial assessment
segments.summary: The example recommends developing an admissions website in-house so students can submit and track applications, view admission status, and communicate with admissions staff. It considers doing nothing and making minor portal improvements, explaining that the larger initiative offers greater financial and operational benefits and better addresses the identified issues. The recommendation includes a five-year financial assessment covering operational and development costs. Development estimates should draw on IT expertise, while financial analysts can help estimate tangible and intangible costs.

segments.label: Rank conference venues using criteria, importance weights, and common-scale ratings
segments.summary: Four potential conference venues are compared using location, facilities, and cost. Location and facilities are divided into more detailed criteria. The example assigns first-level importance weights of 0.35, 0.45, and 0.20, with separate weights within each detailed group. Performance ratings use a scale where 100 represents the best performance and zero the worst. For venue A, environment and transportation ratings of zero and 100 receive equal weights, producing a location rating of 50. That rating is multiplied by the location weight of 0.35 and combined with the other weighted ratings to produce an overall total of 48.8. The resulting totals place B first, followed by D, A, and C. Comparing their performance also reveals trade-offs: B scores highest but is expensive, while C is inexpensive but performs poorly overall. The ranking supports a decision based on what matters to stakeholders; it does not make the highest-scoring option an automatic choice.

segments.label: Sequence releases around goals and revise them as information changes
segments.summary: An online bookstore example groups planned work into releases with different goals. The first release supports validation through a basic end-to-end flow: a home page, title search, adding a book to a shopping cart, and credit-card checkout. A second release aims toward public availability by adding categories, book details, and removal from the cart. If learning shows that customers will not pay by credit card, cash on delivery moves into the second release. Other additions are deferred: further stakeholder-requested features are considered for release three, while PayPal checkout and buying multiple copies of a book are considered for release four. These placements illustrate a sequence that changes with new information, not a universal release plan.

segments.label: Build a narrative with clear headlines and supporting detail
segments.summary: Start with findings and conclusions already established, then organize them into a coherent presentation narrative. The presenter recommends drafting and revising an outline before building slides. Each key statement has supporting evidence beneath it; a homelessness example illustrates this statement-and-evidence structure using different measures over time. Review the argument for audience fit before turning the outline into slide headings and bodies. Headlines should communicate the complete argument when read in sequence, while each slide body should justify its headline. The presenter calls these headlines “action titles” and describes the outline as a “dot-dash” structure. These are ways to connect the main message with the detail that supports it, not requirements to use particular software.

segments.label: A central system, external connected systems, and information exchanges
segments.summary: The example represents a new portal as one central oval and its connected systems as separate rectangles. These connected systems are external to the portal’s boundary, even when they belong to the same organization. Lines describe information exchanged with the portal: for example, the accounting system sends E-Check information into it. Direction is expressed with pass/pull wording; directional arrows are offered as an alternative. An existing resource center appears without a connection because it is being retired. This is a project-specific scope annotation, not a standard requirement for context diagrams. The explanation places context modeling after understanding the business need and before analyzing detailed requirements, so external connections can be considered early.

segments.label: Break an order-entry function into major parts and subparts
segments.summary: An order-entry example uses interview notes to identify three major functions: enter customer data, enter product data, and verify price. Customer data entry includes checking credit status and order history. Product data entry includes checking stock status for the product and quantity entered. Price verification includes checking current promotions, quantity discounts, and price updates. These checks form smaller parts beneath their respective parent functions. Functions can be numbered for reference, and the hierarchy can extend to lower levels when more detail is needed.

segments.label: Keep the right references moving or fixed when copying formulas
segments.summary: Relative references preserve their position relative to the formula: copying =C3*2 changes the referenced cell, while =$C$3*2 continues to use C3. A hypothetical clinic example calculates patients served as booked appointments plus walk-ins minus cancellations, then copies calculations across additional days. A sales-bonus example shows why an entirely relative formula can produce incorrect results when copied. Fixing the sales-amount column and the bonus-rate row with separate dollar signs allows one formula to work across rates and down sales rows. Each dollar sign fixes only the part of the reference it precedes.

segments.label: Inspect and correct formulas copied down and across
segments.summary: A hypothetical app-sales spreadsheet uses SUM to calculate annual totals from quarterly values. Copying the formula down changes its range from B5:E5 to B7:E7. A formula beginning with = divides each app’s annual sales by the overall annual total. Copying initially moves both references; fixing the denominator’s row and column keeps the overall total unchanged while the numerator moves. Dollar signs can be entered manually or cycled with F4. A second calculation divides each quarter’s sales by that app’s annual total. Fully fixing $F$5 works across the first row but incorrectly retains that app’s total when copied down. Using $F5 fixes column F while allowing the row to change. Inspecting destination formulas confirms that copying across and down uses the intended cells.

segments.label: Create a PivotTable and arrange Rows, Values, Columns, and Filters
segments.summary: Creating a PivotTable begins by selecting source data and choosing Insert > PivotTable. The example also converts the source into a named Excel table before opening the PivotTable dialog, which defaults to a new worksheet. Placing salesperson in Rows and amount in Values produces total sales for each salesperson. Amount is summed because this example's field contains numbers. Geography is then added as a second row grouping and moved to create a column-based comparison. Finally, placing geography in Filters provides a control above the report; selecting New Zealand restricts the displayed sales totals to that geography. Field placement determines how the summary answers the business question.

segments.label: Summarize sales by customer and move Region between Filters and Columns
segments.summary: The source sales data is organized with column headers and without intervening empty rows, empty columns, or embedded totals. The example contrasts a fixed source range with an Excel table and explains that newly added table data is reflected after Refresh. A recommended PivotTable creates summed sales by customer on a new worksheet without requiring formulas: customer name occupies Rows and sales USD occupies Values. Value Field Settings changes the calculation to Average and then back to Sum. Number Format adjusts how the summarized numbers appear. Adding Region to Filters allows a region selection; moving it to Columns instead produces customer-by-region totals with grand totals.

segments.label: Find an employee’s job title with XLOOKUP
segments.summary: XLOOKUP retrieves a job title using an employee’s name as the key. The formula supplies the name, the range containing employee names, and the aligned range containing job titles. The creator calls these ranges the lookup array and return array. The returned title is checked against the source data. Referencing the key in cell C3 instead of typing a name directly allows a different employee’s title to be retrieved by changing that cell.

segments.label: Retrieve customer details with VLOOKUP and choose exact matching
segments.summary: VLOOKUP retrieves a customer ID by finding a customer name in the first column of a selected table range and returning column 2. Omitting the final argument defaults to TRUE, which requests approximate matching and expects the lookup column to be sorted. The example produces an incorrect result with unsorted data; sorting corrects that particular result. Using FALSE explicitly requests an exact match, and the returned IDs are checked for two customers. To retrieve a company from column 3, the table range must expand to include that column and the intervening customer ID column.

segments.label: Calculate commission with an IF threshold test
segments.summary: IF uses a logical test to choose between a true result and a false result. In this example, units sold above five earn commission equal to 10% of the total; five or fewer earn 5%. The formula is entered in G2 with the test followed by the two calculations. Changing the units to six recalculates commission at 10%, demonstrating how the selected result changes with the input. The completed formula is then copied down.

segments.label: Summarize sales with PivotTable grouping fields and summed amounts
segments.summary: Create a PivotTable by selecting the source data and using Insert PivotTable. Converting the source range into a named table first helps accommodate future data updates. The PivotTable field areas organize the summary: placing Salesperson in Rows and Amount in Values produces sales totals by salesperson. Excel chooses a sum or count depending on the field; in this example, the numeric Amount field defaults to Sum. Currency formatting and banded rows make the figures easier to read. Adding Geography beneath Salesperson in Rows creates a two-level grouping; moving Geography into Columns provides a matrix layout. Alternatively, placing Geography in Filters restricts the salesperson totals to a selected geography, such as New Zealand.

segments.label: Inspect the outcome and make room for stakeholder feedback
segments.summary: A Sprint Review brings participants, including real end users, together to inspect delivered work and adapt based on what they discover. The example concerns an improved table component for creating and editing broadcasting work orders. The narrator points out that the Product Owner is enthusiastic about showing completed work but has not left enough room for feedback. A demonstration is only the beginning of a review: it should trigger stakeholder feedback rather than end the discussion.

segments.label: Five Whys: trace a machine stoppage to its underlying cause
segments.summary: Five Whys extends a causal chain by asking why each previous explanation occurred. The example traces a machine stoppage through a blown fuse, overload, insufficient bearing lubrication, a pump that fails to draw lubricant, and a worn pump shaft. The underlying cause identified is a missing strainer that allowed metal chips to damage the pump. Following the explanations back toward the stoppage helps check the chain's causal logic. The number of questions is flexible: three or eight may be appropriate if they reach an underlying cause rather than stop at a symptom.

segments.label: A central sales table surrounded by descriptive tables
segments.summary: In a hypothetical chocolate business, a sales table records sales details but cannot alone explain a salesperson’s team, a product’s characteristics, or a geography’s region. Separate salesperson, product, and geography tables supply those descriptions. Connections between the sales table and these surrounding tables form the star structure: business observations sit at the center, with descriptive business-entity tables around them.

segments.label: Fact-table events and dimension-table descriptions
segments.summary: A fact table records business events or activity. The sales example includes IDs linking to other tables, event dates, and numeric measures such as quantity and sales. Fact tables often contain numeric measures used in calculations. Dimension tables describe business entities: the product example includes attributes such as name, category, brand, and color. These descriptions provide context for filtering and grouping results. In sales by category, the sales numbers come from facts, while category comes from a dimension.

segments.label: Single and Both cross-filter directions between related tables
segments.summary: Relationship filter direction determines whether a filter can travel from one table to another. In the sales-and-segments example, Single direction from sales to segments lets a customer filter on sales affect the segments total, but filtering segments does not affect sales. Reversing Single direction reverses which table can filter the other. Both permits filters to propagate in either direction between these two tables. These settings control how related data responds to filtering; neither direction is presented here as a universal requirement.

segments.label: Create a comparison visual and add a year slicer
segments.summary: Selecting sales and customer category fields creates a column chart, which can be changed to a clustered bar chart through Visualizations. Choosing another visual type while the existing chart is selected changes that chart; clicking an empty canvas area first allows a separate visual to be added. A slicer using Year from the date hierarchy is changed to a dropdown, resized, and placed above the chart. Selecting a year updates the comparison. Formatting options adjust axis titles, data labels, chart title, alignment, size, and colors, while hovering over bars reveals additional information.

segments.label: Create a dashboard and place existing worksheet views
segments.summary: A dashboard brings existing worksheet views together. Select New Dashboard, then use the size dropdown to choose Automatic; in this demonstration, that enlarges the canvas. Place worksheet views on the dashboard, including a sheet positioned at the top. Sheet names can be changed from the dashboard or within the worksheets, and the dashboard can be customized further.

segments.label: Select recipients and restrict report sharing permissions
segments.summary: For an already-published report, select Share, enter a recipient, and send a link, optionally with a message. Recipients can find shared reports under Browse > Shared with me. The sharing dialog offers links for people in the organization, people with existing access, or specific people, together with options to allow resharing or building content with the underlying data. In the demonstrated setup, the creator selects specific people and limits them to viewing. After applying the settings and sending the link, its audience is restricted to the named recipients.

segments.label: How a measure adds filters to the visual’s context
segments.summary: The example starts with monthly sales for 2021 in an Excel pivot table. CALCULATE adds an innovative-product filter to the measure, then adds a bulk-purchase filter. These conditions supplement the initial visual filter context. The same principle applies to Power BI visuals: CALCULATE can change the filter context in which a measure is evaluated.

segments.label: Create a calculated field and transform displayed values while preserving the source
segments.summary: Several routes open Tableau’s calculation editor, including Analysis > Create Calculated Field. Naming a field, entering the constant 1, and selecting OK creates a numeric calculated field in the data pane. An equals sign on its icon distinguishes it from an original source field, and the created field is available on another worksheet. A separate example edits a customer first-name field directly in a view to display uppercase text. Adding the original first-name field again shows that the source values remain unchanged. This directly entered calculation is available only in that view.

segments.label: Reuse a published Power BI semantic model across reports
segments.summary: A semantic model holds the data and model logic, including tables, source connections, transformations, relationships, measures, and field formatting. The presenter calls this object a dataset and distinguishes it from a report. After explaining publication to the Power BI service, he creates a report connected to an existing model rather than a separate model of its own. He adds a sales visualization, saves the report, and uses the lineage view to show that one model supplies four reports.

segments.label: Build permission for reports using a shared semantic model
segments.summary: Shared semantic models let report creators reuse a model in a workspace, including for reports stored in another workspace. The presenter uses the term shared datasets. Creating a report from a shared model requires Build permission for the relevant user or group. Reusing existing models across reports helps reduce isolated, separately maintained data definitions.

segments.label: Define typed parameters and a return type
segments.summary: A greeting function returns a string built from a name and an age. Initially, its parameters have no type annotations, so unsuitable values can be passed. Adding String and int parameter types exposes incompatible arguments; supplying a string name and an integer age resolves those errors. Declaring String as the return type also makes returning an integer an error. The returned greeting is stored in a variable and displayed.

segments.label: Declare typed fields and initialize each instance through its constructor
segments.summary: A MenuItem class declares a String title and a double price. Giving these fields fixed initial values makes both newly created instances start with the same values, which member reads confirm. To supply different values for each instance, declare a constructor with the class's name. Ordinary parameters accept arguments but do not automatically assign them to fields. Replacing them with this.title and this.price creates initializing formal parameters that establish the corresponding fields from the positional arguments. The resulting member reads show distinct titles and prices for the two instances.

segments.label: Horizontal arrangement and main-axis versus cross-axis alignment
segments.summary: Row arranges children horizontally, whereas Column arranges them vertically. Three differently sized containers illustrate a Row’s horizontal main axis and vertical cross axis. Setting mainAxisAlignment to spaceBetween separates the children; end and center place the group at the horizontal end or center. Setting crossAxisAlignment to end, center, or start positions the children vertically within the Row. In this example, that vertical alignment uses the Row’s height, established by its tallest child, rather than the full screen height.

segments.label: Select a widget and locate its creation site
segments.summary: The Flutter Inspector provides tools for examining widgets and their layout. Select Widget Mode selects a widget and highlights its node in the widget tree, where the selection can be adjusted. Selecting a widget also takes the IDE to its creation location.

segments.label: Non-nullable types and the nullable question mark
segments.summary: Ordinary Dart types exclude null. Adding `?` makes a type nullable, allowing either a value of that type or null. The examples contrast a non-nullable age with a nullable favorite color. Dart reports a diagnostic when a nullable value is used as though its presence were guaranteed.

segments.label: Conditional member access followed by a fallback
segments.summary: A function calculating an absolute value accepts a nullable argument, so directly calling its `.abs()` member produces a diagnostic. Conditional access with `?.` returns null when the receiver is null, leaving the result nullable. Adding `?? 0` supplies zero when that result is null, satisfying the function’s non-nullable return type.

segments.label: Read and update typed map entries, then reject incompatible keys and values
segments.summary: A Dart map associates keys with values. Bare empty braces create a map, while an empty set needs an explicit set type. The example builds a planets map and examines how its entries determine the inferred key and value types. Explicit Map type arguments constrain keys and values separately. Square brackets read an entry by key; assigning through the same notation updates an existing entry or adds a new one. When the map requires string keys and string values, an integer in either position produces an error rather than being converted.

segments.label: Trace initialization, condition checks, and updates
segments.summary: A conventional Dart for loop initializes an integer counter to zero, checks whether it is less than five, and increases it by one after each iteration. The body reports the current counter value using string interpolation. Each update is followed by another condition check, so the body executes for values zero through four. Once the counter reaches five, the condition is false and repetition ends. Running the example confirms those five reported values.

segments.label: Update local State fields and rebuild displayed values with setState
segments.summary: Two integer fields in a State object hold coffee strength and sugar count, initially set to one. Text widgets display these values through string interpolation, with const removed from the field-dependent widgets. Button handlers increase each value up to five, then reset strength to one and sugars to zero. Initially, the handlers change the fields but the displayed numbers do not update: changing a field alone does not schedule the needed build. Each mutation is then placed inside a function passed to setState. Testing the buttons again shows the displayed values increasing and resetting as intended. The example connects a local field mutation to a scheduled build that describes the updated value.

segments.label: Extract a button with configurable content and a caller-provided callback
segments.summary: Two buttons share styling but have different content and actions. A dedicated StyledButton StatelessWidget centralizes the styling and accepts required constructor inputs: a final Widget child and a final void Function() onPressed callback. Its build method forwards those inputs to the underlying button, so callers supply the content and action rather than hardcoding them in the reusable widget. Both existing buttons are replaced with StyledButton instances using their respective inputs. The example also switches from FilledButton to TextButton and changes the corner styling; it demonstrates parameter and callback forwarding, not exact preservation of the original appearance.

segments.label: Share a Row’s remaining width using Expanded and flex factors
segments.summary: Three containers in a Row receive padding, colors, and text so their widths are visible. Wrapping only the first container in Expanded makes it occupy the width left after the other two children take their content-sized widths. Wrapping all three in Expanded gives them equal shares. Setting their flex factors to 3, 2, and 1 changes those shares: the factors total six, so the children receive three-sixths, two-sixths, and one-sixth of the available width—one-half, one-third, and one-sixth.

segments.label: Stack paint order and non-positioned children
segments.summary: Stack lets widgets overlap in shared space. It paints the children in list order, placing later children above earlier ones. By default, its size fits its non-positioned children; an expanding configuration can instead fill the parent's available space. Children initially align at topStart, which depends on text direction. The alignment property changes alignment for non-positioned or partially positioned children, while Positioned gives an individual child a particular placement.

segments.label: Positioned edge offsets and dimensions
segments.summary: Wrap a Stack child in Positioned to control its placement with top, bottom, left, and right, and its dimensions with height and width. One demonstrated placement is 25 units from the top and 50 from the left; another is 25 from the right and 50 from the bottom. Positioned.fill is also introduced as a way to fill the Stack's space.

segments.label: Use LayoutBuilder to select narrow and wide layouts
segments.summary: A reusable StatelessWidget accepts two widget bodies through its constructor. Its LayoutBuilder uses constraints.maxWidth to choose between them: below 600 it returns the narrow body; otherwise it returns the wide body, including at exactly 600. The example gives the bodies different background colors and resizes the available space to demonstrate the change. The creator calls these bodies mobile and desktop; the selection actually depends on available width, not device identity.

segments.label: Repair enlarged text that runs out of space in a Row
